inc wall of text - tl;dr thoughts about replacing income, payroll and capital gains taxes with with a national property tax in a revenue neutral manner

I've been thinking about this for a while now and it always seemed like a sensible idea. I'm hoping that people who know more about economics than I do can discuss this so I can get better educated about the subject.

Unless you are an all out anarchist you have to acknowledge that one of the most important functions of government is to enforce property rights. And it follows that those who own more property are benefiting proportionally more from this service than those who own less. So it makes sense that owners of property should be the ones who contribute to toward a functioning government in proportion to the amount of property they control.

According to this 2009 article the total value of the US economy at the time was 188 trillion http://rutledgecapital.com/2009/05/24/total-assets-of-the-us-economy-188-trillion-134xgdp/ . And according to this site the US Federal direct revenue for 2009 was about 2.1 trillion http://www.usgovernmentrevenue.com/revenue_chart_2005_2020USr_16s1li111lcn_F0f

What would the rate be?

Napkin math and rounding gives a number 1.1% as the necessary "property tax" rate to be revenue neutral with the current system. The real number would probably have to be a bit higher to account for overhead costs but not significantly.

What is meant by "Property"

Property would include all "real" property (land, buildings, vehicles, capital goods, "expensive" personal property), all financial assets like bank accounts, all investment vehicles like stocks and bonds, and intellectual property (discussed further down).

Why is this a good idea?

  1. the tax burden would shift from labor to capital which is a fundamentally more "fair" way to finance the government
  2. politicians would have less power to use the tax code to favor those with political connections at the expense of those who don't
  3. harder to evade AND such a low rate there would be little motivation to do so

Intellectual Property

Intellectual property is an interesting case since it is difficult to accurately assess the value. There would need to be a market based solution. One idea I came up with is all intellectual property is automatically up for auction every year. The assessed value of the intellectual property would be equal to the winning bid. After the auction closed the IP owner would be required to either pay the property tax rate on the winning bid amount OR sell the IP to the winning bidder, at which point the winning bidder becomes liable for the tax. There would have to be criminal penalties for putting in false bids similar to any other kind of fraud.

For example Pepsi could put in a bid on the Coca Cola trademarked logo of 1 billion dollars. Then Coca Cola would either pay the tax of 11 million based on the previously assumed rate OR they could sell the logo to Pepsi who would have to pay Coca Cola the 1 billion then pay the tax of 11 million.

An alternative to the auctions brought up by qtm in the comments is to have the IP owner decide the value. Then anyone would have the option of paying that price to the owner to acquire the IP rights and assume the tax liability. If nobody wanted to buy the IP at that price then the owner would pay the tax. This would be much less complicated to implement than an auction system and would avoid any enforcement issues caused by bad-faith bidding.

The Farm Problem

The farm problem is that some very capital intensive operations don't generate much revenue relative to the value of the equipment/land required. For these even the very low tax rate couldn't be paid. An idea for these kinds of "nationally vital" businesses is that the taxes would be allowed to be deferred (with reasonable interest) until the property is transferred to a non-immediate-family member at which point the taxes become due.

Capital Flight

There is the possible risk of capital fleeing overseas but phasing the tax in gradually enough would decrease the rate at which this would happen. A cruder solution would be impose a relatively high (compared to the tax rate) penalty on moving money out of the country that would be phased out over time.
